Personally, I hope the government will let capitalism run its course; if they can’t systematically turn a profit, why should the taxpayers come to their rescue?

items.content:
There have been rumors that open-source AI could soon be limited and regulated. I believe the opposite is what’s needed: we need more open-source AI, not less, for everyone, from all over the world, at the frontier and everywhere!

Open models mean more control and transparency over our technology, cheaper AI that we can adapt to our needs and ability to compete with the big players instead of depending fully on renting intelligence from them. 

Restricting open models wouldn’t make AI safer. It would simply hide the risks, concentrate power in the hands of a few and make it harder for the next generation of builders, researchers, academia, non-profits, governments to participate in making AI safer and more beneficial for all.

If you agree and want to show support, we're organizing a peaceful and joyful meetup or march in San Francisco on Saturday. Please join and spread the word!

items.title:
A connected factory without control is just a faster way to make mistakes.

When machines share live...
items.content:
A connected factory without control is just a faster way to make mistakes.

When machines share live data, every signal can affect production, so automation needs purpose, reliable data, and clear human responsibility.

Microblog  by  @antgrasso  about  #SmartManufacturing  #IoT

The point is simple: connecting machines does not automatically make a factory smarter.

A connection is useful when it helps production work better, improves maintenance, or makes the process safer.

Data is where many problems start.

If sensor data is wrong, late, or poorly protected, automated systems can act with confidence on bad information.

In a factory, that can affect quality and safety very quickly.

Security also needs to move closer to the shop floor.

Remote access, controllers, and industrial networks are no longer background infrastructure.

They are part of the production system.

This is why IT and OT cannot work as separate worlds.

Connected production needs shared rules and visible responsibility, so people can understand who owns the data, who controls the process, and how automated decisions are checked.

Chinese cars are better and cheaper, so no one needs Volkswagen cars in China and the rest of the world. German cars no longer live up to their reputation for the best quality and reliability. I'm speaking as a frustrated VW owner who was fooled by the "German car reputation" fairy tale.

Half of the board at @VW is controlled by the union, and the other half is controlled by the shareholders. This means that the unions, whose leaders aren't interested in the company's survival and are only interested in keeping the status quo, will block any shareholders' initiatives.

Labor unions that were created in the West under pressure from the Soviet Union contributed to the drastic improvement of the working conditions of Western workers, but in a reality where they aren't needed anymore because the legislation does the job, unions are like the facehugger that squeezes the throat of the host when you try to reduce the union's grip on the business it is bullying.

When legislation protects workers well enough and democracy works, unions must be disbanded. Otherwise, the entire national economy will suffocate under the pressure from China and other countries where working conditions and energy costs allow for higher margins.

@stedmanhalliday @joshmobleymusic @Sonos I forget all the details.

But he told me about speaker clipping. Back in the old days, if you had too powerful an amplifier, you could put so much charge onto the magnet coil that it would shove the speaker cone out of its channel (or whatever they call it). 

He said these new modern speakers, they get the spec sheet and they can program them to operate optimally at different volume levels all the way up to 100%. So he said, "I've designed the speaker to sound pretty good all the way turned up." 

When I was a kid, if you turned up your amplifier all the way, you would have blown something.
